name: LMD18200T_NOPB
title: LMD18200: 3 A, 55 V H-bridge
summary: A single full H-bridge for DC and stepper motors, four DMOS switches of 0.33 Ω typical each with bipolar/CMOS control on one die, rated 3 A continuous and 6 A peak from a 12 V to 55 V supply. Three logic inputs (DIRECTION, BRAKE, PWM) suit locked anti-phase or sign/magnitude PWM. It has a current-sense output of 377 µA per ampere, a thermal warning flag at 145 °C, shutdown at 170 °C, shorted-load protection and an internal charge pump that can be speeded up with two 10 nF bootstrap capacitors. It comes in an 11-lead TO-220.

pins.name: BOOTSTRAP1
pins.function: Bootstrap capacitor node for half-bridge 1; 10 nF goes from this pin to pin 2.

pins.name: DIRECTION
pins.function: Logic input that sets which way current flows between OUTPUT1 and OUTPUT2, and so the motor's direction; with BRAKE high it picks which pair of switches shorts the load (truth table).

pins.name: BRAKE
pins.function: Logic input. High, with PWM also high, shorts the motor through both high-side switches (DIRECTION high) or both low-side switches (DIRECTION low). High with PWM low turns every output switch off, leaving about −1.5 mA of bias current at each output.

pins.name: PWM
pins.function: Logic input; its role, together with DIRECTION, depends on the PWM format used (locked anti-phase or sign/magnitude).

pins.name: GROUND
pins.function: Ground return; tied inside the package to the mounting tab.

pins.name: CURRENT_SENSE
pins.function: Current output proportional to the current in the high-side (sourcing) switches, typically 377 µA per ampere.

pins.name: THERMAL_FLAG
pins.function: Open-collector thermal warning output; goes low when the junction reaches 145 °C. The outputs are not shut down until 170 °C.

pins.name: BOOTSTRAP2
pins.function: Bootstrap capacitor node for half-bridge 2; 10 nF goes from this pin to pin 10.

circuits.title: Test circuit
circuits.description: The bridge drives two 12 Ω loads, one from OUTPUT2 up to VS and one from OUTPUT1 down to ground, so the sinking and sourcing switching times can be measured at 3 A from a 42 V supply. PWM is held at +5 V, BRAKE is grounded and the test pulse goes to DIRECTION. Both half-bridges have 10 nF bootstrap capacitors, VS is decoupled by 1 µF and 1200 µF to pin 7, and the sense output works into 2.7 kΩ to ground.

circuits.title: Fixed off-time control
circuits.description: Chopper current control in sign/magnitude mode for a 24 V, 3 A DC motor. The sense current from pin 8 develops a voltage on 2 kΩ (filtered by 0.1 µF) that one LM393 comparator holds against the MAG command, scaled 1.33 A per volt. When the motor current passes the command the comparator output falls and triggers an LM555 monostable; for TOFF = 1.1 RC the 555 output is high, the second comparator pulls PWM low, and the motor terminals see zero average voltage. The current therefore ripples a little about the commanded level. An LM340LA-12 makes 12 V for the control parts from the 24 V rail. DIR takes the forward or reverse signal; BRAKE is grounded.
notes: U3 is a dual comparator: pins 1, 2, 3 are one comparator (output, −, +), pins 7, 6, 5 the other, 8 the supply and 4 ground.
TOFF = 1.1 RC, set by RT and CT on the LM555.

circuits.title: Torque regulation, locked anti-phase
circuits.description: An LM3524D PWM controller closes a current loop around a brushed 24 V DC motor run in locked anti-phase: its output (pin 13, pulled up by 10 kΩ) passes through an exclusive-OR gate whose other input is the direction control, and drives DIRECTION, while PWM is tied to +10 V. The sense output of pin 8 into 6.19 kΩ, 1 % with 0.1 µF across it is the feedback to the controller's pin 2; the 1 kΩ potentiometer under 300 Ω from +10 V sets VCURRENT ADJUST on pin 1, so peak motor current follows the adjust voltage. 3.6 kΩ and 10 nF set the controller's oscillator and 1 nF compensates it. Each half-bridge has a 10 nF bootstrap capacitor, the 12 V to 24 V motor supply is bypassed by 220 µF and 1 µF, BRAKE is grounded, and the thermal flag is pulled up to +10 V by 10 kΩ.

parts.value: 24 V DC motor, 0.25 A to 3.25 A

notes: Peak motor current against VCURRENT ADJUST is the curve Peak Motor Current vs Adjustment Voltage.

circuits.title: Velocity regulation with tachometer feedback
circuits.description: The same LM3524D locked anti-phase drive as the torque loop, with motor speed as the feedback. A tachometer generator on the motor (1000 RPM per volt) sits in a four-diode network; its output, divided by 10 kΩ over 5.1 kΩ, goes to the controller's pin 2. The speed command on pin 1 comes from a 1 kΩ potentiometer fed from the controller's pin 16 through three series diodes, with one diode under the potentiometer to ground; the top of the potentiometer also returns the far side of the tachometer network. The current-sense output is not used. Motor speed against the control voltage is the curve Motor Speed vs Control Voltage.

parts.value: 24 V DC motor, 0.25 A to 3.25 A

operation.text: A full H-bridge of four DMOS power switches with bipolar and CMOS control on one die. Each half-bridge has a high-side (sourcing) and a low-side (sinking) switch; the control logic prevents shoot-through. Built in: clamp diodes, shorted-load protection, a thermal warning flag at 145 °C, thermal shutdown at 170 °C, undervoltage lockout (outputs off between 9 V and 11 V), a charge pump for the high-side gates with the option of external bootstrap capacitors, and a low-loss current-sense output. Inputs accept TTL and CMOS levels. Up to 3 A continuous and 6 A peak.

BRAKE high with PWM high shorts the motor terminals: DIRECTION high turns both sourcing switches on, DIRECTION low both sinking switches. BRAKE high with PWM low turns all four switches off; each output then carries only a bias current of about −1.5 mA. With BRAKE low, PWM low turns both sourcing switches on.

One PWM signal carries both direction and amplitude. It drives DIRECTION (pin 3) while PWM (pin 5) is held high. At 50 % duty cycle the average voltage across the load over a period is zero, so drive is zero.

Direction and amplitude are separate signals: the sign goes to DIRECTION (pin 3) and the duty-cycle-modulated magnitude to PWM (pin 5). A steady low on PWM means zero drive, and load current scales with pulse width.

Edges on DIRECTION, BRAKE and PWM should not coincide: leave at least 1 µs between transitions on different inputs. A conservative rule is at least 500 ns from the end of one transition to the start of the next. Minimum input pulse width is 1 µs typical.

Pin 8 sources 377 µA per ampere of output current (typical). The resistor from pin 8 to ground should be sized so pin 8 stays at or below 5 V for best accuracy and linearity; the pin's voltage compliance is 12 V. Only current through the upper, sourcing switches is sensed; freewheeling (recirculating) current is not. Accuracy against load current and junction temperature is given by the Current Sense Operating Region curve (7 % and 10 % boundaries).

Pin 9 is an open-collector output, so flags from several devices can be wired-OR and the high level set by the external pull-up. It goes low at a junction temperature of 145 °C; shutdown follows at 170 °C. Typical use is an interrupt to the system controller, which can then cut load current or shut the system down in order. The pin's voltage compliance is 12 V.

Fast current steps during switching cause voltage transients across stray supply inductance, so bypass VS to GROUND with high-quality capacitance as close to pins 6 and 7 as possible: the recommended part is a 1 µF ceramic of good high-frequency quality. Keep supply transients below the 60 V absolute maximum. Above 40 V of supply a transient voltage suppressor such as a P6KE62A from supply to ground is recommended, and the ceramic capacitor can usually be left out. At high load current at least 100 µF per ampere of load is generally needed to absorb the recirculating current of inductive loads.

Protection circuitry watches for surge current from a shorted load, with a threshold of about 10 A, and turns the power switch off as fast as it can. In a motor drive the usual faults are shorted windings and a locked rotor; the motor's inductance, and any inductance in series with the supply, keeps the surge to a level the device survives. After shutdown the device periodically tries to turn the switch back on, so normal running resumes once the fault clears; while the fault remains it cycles in and out of thermal shutdown, which puts transients on the supply that good bypassing must handle. A hard short from an output to ground is the worst case: around 15 A can flow and the die and package may dissipate up to 500 W for the brief time before shutdown, which can destroy the part, more so above 30 V. Good heat sinking is essential, and the VS pin (pin 6) normally needs 1 square inch of PCB copper as a heat sink.

The high-side DMOS gates must be driven about 8 V above the supply. An internal charge pump does this: an internal capacitor is charged to about 14 V while switched to ground, then switched to the supply, lifting the gate drive above it. A free-running internal 300 kHz oscillator clocks it. The gate-drive rise time is about 20 µs, good for switching up to 1 kHz.

For faster switching, a 10 nF capacitor from each output to its bootstrap pin (pin 2 to pin 1, pin 10 to pin 11) acts as a second, larger charge pump, switched by the power switches themselves. It charges the power switch's gate capacitance quickly, giving rise times typically under 100 ns and switching frequencies up to 500 kHz. The bootstrap pins are rated to VOUT + 16 V.

Each of the four switches has its own diode that clamps inductive transients beyond the supply or ground to one diode drop across the switch (1.2 V typical, 1.5 V maximum at 3 A). Recovery matters: with 6 A forward current, the diodes across the sourcing switches recover in about 70 ns with 1 A of reverse recovery current, those across the sinking switches in about 100 ns with 4 A. The switches must carry that recovery current.

Quiescent supply current is 13 mA typical, 25 mA maximum, with all logic inputs low at 42 V. It rises with switching frequency (about 13.5 mA at 1 kHz to about 17.7 mA at 100 kHz) and falls with junction temperature.
ESD protection on chip is limited. In storage and handling, short the leads together or keep the part in conductive foam so the MOS gates are not damaged.
The tab is connected to GROUND, pin 7.
